blocks.md: Most engineers meet Claude Code expecting fancy autocomplete. They open the terminal, type *'add a login button'*, watch it run for forty minutes, and either get something brilliant or something that touched 14 files including the build config. Both outcomes feel like luck because both **are** luck. Claude Code rewards a specific working style: plan first, then execute, with a kernel file that remembers your standards. Without that, you are running a fast junior on caffeine in your filesystem at 2am. With it, Claude Code shipping work is the most leveraged hour of your day.

blocks.title: Mental model: Claude Code is a plan-then-execute teammate
blocks.md: Picture a junior engineer pair-programming with you. Before they touch a file they say *'so the plan is: change the User type, then update three call sites, then add a migration, then run the tests'*. You nod or push back. Then they execute, narrating as they go. If you skip the plan step you are not pair-programming; you are watching a junior wing it on the keyboard. Claude Code is exactly the same. **The plan is not a bureaucratic step; the plan is what makes the execution sane**.

hi-IN.title: Pune SaaS ka migration story
hi-IN.md: Scene yeh hai: Pune ki ek B2B SaaS, 18-engineer team. Tech lead ne Claude Code ko bola *'migrate karo Express se Fastify'*. 47 minute baad, 84 files badal chuke the, build broken, half the routes 500-ing. Tech lead ne git reset kara, **CLAUDE.md likha**, plan-first kara, fir bola karo. 11 din lage but zero rollback. Lesson? Bina plan, Claude Code ek confident junior hai jisko keys de di. Plan ke saath, woh tumse 3x faster ship karta hai.

en.title: The Pune migration that worked the second time
en.md: A Pune SaaS asked Claude Code to migrate from Express to Fastify in one shot. 84 files later, the build was broken and half the routes were 500-ing. They git reset, wrote a CLAUDE.md kernel, ran /plan first, then /implement. The second pass took 11 days with zero rollback. Same model, same task, completely different outcome.

blocks.md:
Every non-trivial task should start with a planning subagent that reads code and writes a plan, **without modifying anything**. The built-in `Plan` subagent does exactly this. It investigates the codebase, asks clarifying questions, and produces `docs/PLAN.md` in a canonical format: goal, files touched, approach, risks, rollback. Then a separate run executes the plan.

Why split? Three reasons. First, **planning catches contradictions** before they become 14 broken files. Second, **the plan is reviewable in two minutes** while the diff is reviewable in two hours. Third, **a paused plan is cheap to throw away**; a half-done execution is expensive. Run `/plan` for anything that touches 3+ files, anything in auth or payments or migrations, and anything where you are not 100 percent sure of the right approach. Run it even when you are sure; you will be surprised how often you were wrong.

steps.label: /plan
steps.body: Ask Claude Code to produce a plan: which routes, which DB tables, which env vars, which idempotency strategy, which retry behaviour, which test cases.

steps.label: Review
steps.body: Read the PLAN.md. Push back: 'we already have an events table, reuse it' or 'do not add a new env var'.

steps.label: /implement
steps.body: Run the doer. Sonnet 4.6 with the plan as context. Tell it to follow the plan strictly and stop if it deviates.

steps.label: Inline review
steps.body: Read every diff. The plan said 4 files; if 7 changed, ask why before approving.

steps.label: Test
steps.body: Tests run automatically in a pre-commit hook (configured in CLAUDE.md). Failed test = stop.

steps.label: Commit
steps.body: You commit, not Claude. The kernel hook blocks autonomous commits anyway.

blocks.prompt: When is /plan most clearly NOT worth the overhead?

choices.label: Renaming a single function in one file with no callers
choices.explain: Single-file, single-change, zero blast radius. Just do it. /plan is for the cases where 'just do it' burns hours of cleanup.

choices.label: Adding a new payment provider
choices.explain: Payments are exactly the case where you must plan. The trap is thinking 'just plug it in'.

choices.label: Refactoring a 200-file codebase
choices.explain: Largest possible blast radius. Plan, fan out into subagents, do not freestyle.

choices.label: Writing a database migration
choices.explain: Migrations on a live DB are the highest-risk single change in the kernel. Always plan.

hi-IN.title: Tutorial Tuesday wala intern
hi-IN.md: Bhai, ek intern aaya, sweet boy, tutorial dekh ke aaya. Pehle hi din Claude Code se bola *'production-ready auth bana do, sab features'*. Claude Code ne 6 packages install kiye, .env file mein 11 keys daali (kaha se aayi pata nahi), 23 files banaye. Senior dev ne PR khola, samjha 30 minute, fir delete kiya pura. Lesson? CLAUDE.md mein likh do *'auth changes need /plan first, no new env vars without ENV.md update'*. Phir Claude rules pe chalega, vibes pe nahi.

en.title: Production-ready auth in one prompt
en.md: An intern asked Claude Code for production-ready auth in one prompt. It installed 6 packages, invented 11 environment variables, and created 23 files. The senior spent 30 minutes understanding it, then deleted everything. The fix is not 'never use Claude Code'; it is to write CLAUDE.md rules that say 'auth changes need /plan' and 'no new env vars without docs entry'. Rules are cheaper than reviews.

blocks.md:
CLAUDE.md is a markdown file at the root of your repo that Claude Code reads at the start of every session. It is your **kernel** in the Linux sense: a small, durable, always-loaded set of rules that constrain everything else. A good kernel has six things: stack nouns, key commands, hard rules (MUST / SHOULD / MAY), slash commands, load-on-demand pointers to deeper docs, and known issues.

What does this buy you? **Reproducibility**. Two different engineers running Claude Code on your repo get the same standards. **Speed**. Common protocols collapse to one slash command. **Safety**. The hard-rules section blocks the things that would otherwise need a code review to catch. Claude Code without CLAUDE.md is just expensive autocomplete. Claude Code with a 200-line kernel is a teammate who has read your style guide, your testing strategy, and the postmortems.

intro: Engineering team is fighting about what goes in CLAUDE.md. Some want everything; some want nothing. Both are wrong.
Sort each item into KERNEL (every session), MODULE DOC (loaded when relevant), or NOWHERE.

buckets.label: NOWHERE — does not belong in CLAUDE

scenarios.situation: The list of allowed UI library components
scenarios.explain: Belongs in docs/STYLE.md, loaded when the task touches UI. Too long for the kernel.
Hard rule, must be re-read every session, low cost to keep top-of-mind.
TODOs belong in your tracker, not in a file every Claude session reads.
Secrets never go in CLAUDE.md. Most editors auto-include it in the LLM context.

scenarios.situation: How to structure a Prisma migration
scenarios.explain: docs/DATABASE.md, loaded when a task touches the schema.

scenarios.situation: The slash command /plan and when to use it
scenarios.explain: Slash commands collapse repeated protocols into one token. Belongs in the kernel.

blocks.title: The classic trap: the unbounded subagent
blocks.md: Subagents are powerful: `general-purpose` for multi-step research, `Plan` for read-only planning, `bug-hunter` for finding the root cause of a failure, `pr-reviewer` for reading a diff, `Explore` for codebase orientation. The trap: launching a subagent without a bounded brief and a hard stop. *'Investigate why the build is slow'* is unbounded; *'investigate why the build is slow, focus on the webpack config and the test pipeline, return a 5-bullet diagnosis'* is bounded. Unbounded subagents drift, cost more, and produce essays you have to read. Always give them a brief and a deliverable.

blocks.prompt: Order a clean Claude Code session for a new feature

items.label: Confirm CLAUDE.md is current and STACK.md is filled
items.detail: If kernel is stale, every session is stale.

items.label: Review the plan; push back where wrong
Run /implement with the approved plan as context
items.detail: Doer follows the plan, narrates each step.

items.label: Run /ship for the pre-deploy checklist
items.detail: Typecheck, lint, test, build, staging verify.

blocks.hint: Kernel before plan. Plan before implement. Diff before ship.

blocks.instruction: Write a 6-line CLAUDE.md hard-rules block for a hypothetical Next.js + Prisma + Stripe project. Use MUST / SHOULD / MAY. Be opinionated.
blocks.expected:
## Hard Rules

### MUST
- No secrets in source. process.env only. Hook scans staging.
- No autonomous commits or pushes. Developer commits.

### SHOULD
- Return Result<T,E> from data-layer functions; throw only at framework edges.
- Money as integer cents in the database.

### MAY
- Tailwind class order — prettier-plugin-tailwindcss enforces.
- Conventional Commits — commitlint enforces.

hi-IN.title: run_in_background ka misuse
hi-IN.md: Bhai, run_in_background ek beautiful tool hai. Lambi backfill, batch job, slow integration test — background mein chala do, foreground mein doosra kaam karo. Lekin ek Bengaluru ki team ne **`rm -rf node_modules && npm install` ko background mein chalaya** while foreground was editing package.json. Race condition, half-installed deps, build broke. Lesson? Background = independent task with no shared state. Agar overlap hai, sequential rakho.

en.title: Background isn't a magic word
en.md: A team ran rm -rf node_modules in the background while the foreground agent was editing package.json. Half-installed deps, broken build. run_in_background is for independent tasks with no shared state. Anything that touches the same files as foreground work belongs in sequence.

points: Claude Code without CLAUDE.md is expensive autocomplete; with a kernel it is a teammate.
Always /plan before /implement for anything 3+ files, auth, payments, or migrations.
The plan is reviewable in 2 minutes; the diff is reviewable in 2 hours. Cheaper to be wrong on the plan.
Subagents need bounded briefs and a deliverable; unbounded subagents drift.
Hooks enforce the rules you would otherwise have to enforce in code review.

blocks.prompt: Open your repo. Is there a CLAUDE.md? If not, write one this week with 6 hard rules, 3 slash commands, and 3 load-on-demand pointers. If yes, when did you last update it? Stale kernels are worse than missing ones.
